RT Dario Amodei
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea.

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole.

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

blogs.content:
Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security

If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.

 This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:

 On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]

 As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

 This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:

 August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

 August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.

 August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.

 August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.

 September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.

 October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.

 October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

 Via Hacker News

 Tags: open-source , php , security , ai , ai-security-research

blogs.content:
Listen to this post :

 Log in to listen

 Stratechery is, starting from today, presented by Stripe.

 The Unified Content Business Model

 Readers have, over the years, pointed out the paradox of my belief in and advocacy for advertising-based business models being delivered in a format bereft of advertising. In truth, however, there was no paradox, just pragmatism: when I launched the Stratechery business model I intended on having sponsors, and did for a month or two, before I realized that ad sales for a one-person business with a small audience was a waste of time; I was much better served devoting my attention to content and trusting that readers would be willing to pay.

 And, thankfully, readers were willing to pay, and ultimately, there ended up being far more such readers than I ever dreamed of. In fact, there were so many readers willing to pay that I have, over the subsequent 12 years, been able to build an audience that is uniquely attractive to potential advertisers, along with a team that can help me pursue the multi-faceted business model I always planned on. Stratechery is a business, and subscriptions + advertising is The Unified Content Business Model I have long advocated.

 Embracing Conflict

 That noted, this is a big change, both for you and for me; I’ll start with the latter. I take my ethics policy very seriously, including the fact I am not paid for posts, I do not hold individual stocks, and I pay for all of my own expenses. This has, in all honesty, probably cost me a fair bit of money, but the payoff has been trust from you, and for me the sense of personal integrity this provided.

 To that end, with this announcement, I am editing my ethics policy to include this paragraph:

 Stratechery is, as of October 2026, presented by Stripe, and there I make no claims of objectivity. To the extent I analyze not just Stripe but the entire fintech space, I strive to give my honest opinion; my contract with Stripe contains total editorial independence. However, the reality of a conflict is inescapable, and I will disclose my relationship to Stripe in every post where this conflict may be relevant.

 My ethics policy is going to include a link to this announcement, because there is one more admission to make: if I am honest with myself I have never been truly objective about Stripe specifically, for three reasons.

 First, Stripe is a foundational business for my business. The then-startup launched the Subscription API (what later became Stripe Billing ) in late 2011; Stratechery was predicated on that feature existing (and, I would add, the fact that a novice developer like myself could incorporate the Subscription API spoke to Stripe’s ease-of-use!).

 Second, Stripe is the foundation of Passport, the access management software that undergirds Stratechery, SemiAnalysis’ institutional offerings , and The Ankler ; we have and continue to work with Stripe closely for both Stratechery and Passport.

 Third, I have had the good fortune of becoming friends with Patrick and John Collison, who were some of the earliest Stratechery readers and subscribers.

 I did always try and set these considerations aside when writing about Stripe; in truth I actually just wrote about Stripe and the fintech space less, as I was cognizant about these informal conflicts.

 By the same token, this is exactly why I couldn’t be more thrilled to have Stripe as an exclusive sponsor: if I am informally conflicted, why not make it formal? I actually think this gives me more freedom to write about fintech, not less, because the conflict will be on my sleeve; more than that, however, every ad I run or read is going to be heartfelt: I believe in Stripe, love their service, and while I am being paid for those ads, I will have the satisfaction of truly believing in them as well.

 FAQ

 That leaves the impact on you, the reader, and I’ve made an FAQ:

 Where are ads going to run?

 There are three primary places you will see Stripe ads:

 There is a “Presented by Stripe” placement on Stratechery, the cover art of the Stratechery, Stratechery Interview, and Sharp Tech podcasts, and in the emails I send. I honestly think it looks pretty great, but I’m biased!

 There will be occasional ad placements between sections of the Update, in the Interviews, and between Articles; this will apply to the web, email, and the Stratechery podcast (which is, and will continue to be, simply the audio version of what you can get on the web or via email).

 There will be a segment of Sharp Tech where Andrew and I discuss the Stripe ad topic of the week, along with an acknowledgment at the beginning of an episode, and an ad at the end.

 More on Sharp Tech below.

 What about sponsored content?

 There is no requirement that I run sponsored content; however, I’m actually very excited about the potential of occasionally leveraging Stripe content. Stripe has a unique position in terms of working with companies across the entire economy, and that is particularly true when it comes to AI. You see some of the insights that come from this position on both the Stripe blog and the Stripe Economics blog , and I look forward to incorporating those kinds of insights when it makes sense (and I should also call out Stripe’s Works in Progress site ). Just to be clear, however, that will be my call.

 So Stripe can’t tell you what to write?

 Absolutely not. More than that, Stripe cannot tell me what not to write either. I could call for Patrick Collison’s firing and I’m still going to get paid.

 I am not, for the record, going to do that; as I noted I will disclose this relationship whenever it seems relevant. However, my first loyalty is to my readers; that meant absolute editorial independence was a prerequisite for this deal.

 Can I skip the ads if I’m a subscriber?

 No. Like I said above, Stratechery is a business, and it’s the quality of my audience that makes this deal possible. Moreover, Stratechery has never promised to be ad-free: what I am selling is access to my paid content, and it’s on me to make that content worthwhile. In fact, I would spin this the other way: my motivation to deliver great content is higher than ever, knowing that it has to be worth not just your money but also the attention that I have chosen to share with a sponsor.

 That noted, while I don’t make categorical statements about my business, I do not anticipate raising subscription prices again, and certainly not over the course of this deal.

 Do I get anything out of this deal?

 This is the part I’m most excited about: I am going to invest the revenue from this deal into making more and better products. I have a bunch of ideas that are now unlocked, and one of them is launching this week: in-person Sharp Tech.

 The New Sharp Tech

 I am extremely excited to announce that, starting this week, Sharp Tech will become a video podcast, recorded live and in-person. Over the past couple of months I have been building a small video studio in my home, and Andrew will be flying to Wisconsin every week (when possible) to make what I strongly believe will be a better product. There is no matching the energy and chemistry that comes from recording in person, so we’re going to do exactly that the majority of the time.

 We will be posting video episodes on YouTube (for clarity, not live as we record, at least to start), as well as through existing feeds; these episodes will be free. In addition, we will be adding a second weekly mailbag-centric audio-only episode — recorded the same day, in-person — for subscribers only.

 This is the first of what I hope will be many product launches for subscribers; my goal is that this sponsorship is seen as a real unlock and accelerant for what it means to be not just a subscriber but a member of the best audience in the world. That’s what I believe I have, it’s what Stripe believes that I have, and I’m grateful to every one of you for making that a reality and this business possible.

blogs.title: The GPU Revenue Ladder
blogs.description: Yesterday brought two data points about the health of inference businesses : SpaceX’s third-quarter report1 & DeepSeek’s inference post.2 Ov…
blogs.content:
Yesterday brought two data points about the health of inference businesses : SpaceX’s third-quarter report 1 & DeepSeek’s inference post. 2

 Overall, they demonstrate that inference businesses can be quite healthy even at current prices & efficiencies. Plus there is a tremendous amount of upside assuming demand persists at higher prices per card hour.

 Rung
 $/card-hour
 Change from above
 Provenance

 Theoretical maximum revenue, DeepSeek
 $38.00
 —
 company claim, theoretical

 Spot price, B200
 $8.77
 −77%
 ORNN, settled 2026-10-20

 Negotiated price, SpaceX
 $5.27
 −40%
 S-1, implied

 Realized revenue, SpaceX
 $2.44
 −54%
 8-K, derived

 DeepSeek calculates a $38 maximum per GPU card-hour. 3 It describes a GPU running under optimal conditions : maximum utilization for external customers rather than internal work, & 100% of its output usable & billable, sold at full list price.

 Revenue may be lower because V3 is priced below R1, & because prices vary between peak & off-peak hours. 4

 The spot price, what it costs to rent a card on the open market today, is $8.77. 5 SpaceX provides us with both the negotiated price from its contracts, at $5.27, 6 as well as the overall realized revenue, including operations costs, training, unusable & unbillable work. 7

 “At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year.”

 — Bret Johnsen, CFO, SpaceX Q3 2026 earnings call

 Assuming the quote measures payback after tax, on fully loaded costs, these economics suggest that the inference business can be a very good one. 8

 But the case rests on demand persisting, & on efficiency outrunning price cuts. The forces pushing the other way are considerable.

 GPU rental prices doubled in six months, from $4.40 to $8.08 per card hour, while the price of intelligence fell much faster. OpenAI cut Luna 80% in July & another 50% in September. A benchmark threshold that cost $0.55 eighteen months ago now clears at $0.0015, a 377-fold reduction. 9 If tokens deflate that quickly while cards cost more, gross profit per card hour depends entirely on throughput gains keeping pace.

 The second force moves inference off the datacenter altogether. AI companies are asking Qualcomm to run large models on the handset itself.

 “Some of the companies at the forefront of AI are telling Qualcomm, by 2028, I need to make sure that I have the ability to run at least a hundred billion parameter model into a phone.”

 — Cristiano Amon, CEO, Qualcomm, on the Sources podcast

 Inference running on laptops & phones never sends tokens to the cloud. 10

 But the cloud is not big enough to support demand, & new data centres are behind schedule, with GPUs sitting idle on warehouse floors waiting for power. 11 JPMorgan finds that more than 60% of the data centre capacity planned for 2027 is not yet under construction, & a further 7% is delayed. 12 With demand continuing to drive record revenue growth for AI, the deflationary forces may succumb to too much demand.

 The economics of large scale inference suggest the business model is healthy at scale, & token factories benefit from more rungs to climb on the pricing ladder.

---

 Space Exploration Technologies Corp., Form 8-K for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, filed October 20, 2026, Exhibit 99.1. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026066482/0001628280-26-066482-index.htm   ↩︎

 DeepSeek’s V4.1-Flash disclosure, which reports revenue of about $38 per card-hour at off-peak prices & roughly $0.60 per million tokens. The figure describes a single best cluster running its cheapest model, not a fleet average. DeepSeek’s earlier V3/R1 overview, from open-source week in February 2025, implied about $12.90 per card-hour: $562,027 of notional daily revenue against $87,072 of daily cost on 1,814 GPUs. https://github.com/deepseek-ai/open-infra-index/blob/main/202502OpenSourceWeek/day_6_one_more_thing_deepseekV3R1_inference_system_overview.md   ↩︎

 Every figure here is an estimate. No company in this table publishes a per-card-hour revenue figure as such. SpaceX’s are derivations from filings & DeepSeek’s is explicitly theoretical.  ↩︎

 Revenue may be lower than the maximum because V3 is priced below R1, & because prices vary between peak & off-peak hours. See note 3.  ↩︎

 ORNN Compute Price Index, settled 2026-10-20. A volume-weighted winsorized mean of executed neocloud transactions, excluding reserved & forward contracts.  ↩︎

 S-1 & S-1/A, 2026 : $1.25b divided by 325,000 GPUs times 730.5 hours equals $5.27. The GPU count & whether the contract bundles power or shells make this an upper bound on pure compute.  ↩︎

 Q3 2026 8-K : AI segment revenue of $7,560m annualized & divided by 1.7 GW. The figure uses installed rather than utilized capacity. The Q2 10-Q defines nameplate as not representing actual utilization.  ↩︎

 Payback is capex divided by annual cash flow, where cash flow is revenue less cash operating costs. Depreciation is excluded from the denominator because the capex is already the numerator. Per card, a $46 per watt build costs $55,200, while the $5.27 contract rate yields $46,165 of annual revenue against roughly $570 of cash operating cost, giving a payback of 1.21 years. At B200 spot the payback is 0.72 years. To reconcile the quote with a $46 per watt build, we assume Johnsen is measuring after tax. At a 21% federal rate, 100% bonus depreciation shields $11,592 in year one, lifting first-year cash flow to $57,187 & shortening payback to 0.97 years. That is a timing benefit rather than a cost reduction : total deductions over the asset’s life are unchanged, so it flatters a payback metric far more than it improves net present value. SpaceX has not disclosed whether the figure is pre- or after-tax, state taxes would raise the shield, & the availability of full bonus depreciation for datacenter property placed in service in 2026 should be verified rather than assumed.  ↩︎

 How GPU Prices Can Double While AI Gets Cheaper . The 377x figure comes from Epoch AI, The Plunging Price of Thought . Luna pricing from GPT-5.6 . Microsoft’s 90% tokens-per-GPU-year from $555B of Cloud Spend .  ↩︎

 Cristiano Amon, Qualcomm, interviewed by Alex Heath on the Sources podcast, published October 8, 2026. He did not name the companies. Qualcomm’s current flagship can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model locally, so a hundred billion parameters is roughly a three-fold jump within about two years.  ↩︎

 Business Insider, October 20, 2026 : Amazon is taking ownership of Nvidia GB300 racks under a program AWS calls “Early Rack Receipt,” before the sites to run them are ready. An internal email projected roughly $5 billion of GB300 deliveries in August alone, & about $3 billion a month thereafter, with some facilities holding space for more racks but lacking the power to activate them. Amazon described staging hardware near deployment sites as standard practice. https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-nvidia-ai-gpu-data-centers-power-shortages-2026-10   ↩︎

 JPMorgan, cited by the Wall Street Journal in June 2026 : more than 60% of data centre capacity planned for completion in 2027 is not yet under construction, & a further 7% is delayed. Goldman Sachs Commodities Research put on-time delivery for the next one to two years at only 50% to 60%, against a historical base rate of roughly 72% for capacity scheduled within four quarters.  ↩︎

blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Stratechery is now presented by Stripe. What that means for me, for you, and for the future of Stratechery content.
blogs.content:
Stratechery is now presented by Stripe. What that means for me, for you, and for the future of Stratechery content.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Stratechery is, starting from today, presented by Stripe.

The Unified Content Business Model

Readers have, over the years, pointed out the paradox of my belief in and advocacy for advertising-based business models being delivered in a format bereft of advertising. In truth, however, there was no paradox, just pragmatism: when I launched the Stratechery business model I intended on having sponsors, and did for a month or two, before I realized that ad sales for a one-person business with a small audience was a waste of time; I was much better served devoting my attention to content and trusting that readers would be willing to pay.

And, thankfully, readers were willing to pay, and ultimately, there ended up being far more such readers than I ever dreamed of. In fact, there were so many readers willing to pay that I have, over the subsequent 12 years, been able to build an audience that is uniquely attractive to potential advertisers, along with a team that can help me pursue the multi-faceted business model I always planned on. Stratechery is a business, and subscriptions + advertising is The Unified Content Business Model I have long advocated.

Embracing Conflict

That noted, this is a big change, both for you and for me; I’ll start with the latter. I take my ethics policy very seriously, including the fact I am not paid for posts, I do not hold individual stocks, and I pay for all of my own expenses. This has, in all honesty, probably cost me a fair bit of money, but the payoff has been trust from you, and for me the sense of personal integrity this provided.

To that end, with this announcement, I am editing my ethics policy to include this paragraph:

Stratechery is, as of October 2026, presented by Stripe, and there I make no claims of objectivity. To the extent I analyze not just Stripe but the entire fintech space, I strive to give my honest opinion; my contract with Stripe contains total editorial independence. However, the reality of a conflict is inescapable, and I will disclose my relationship to Stripe in every post where this conflict may be relevant.

My ethics policy is going to include a link to this announcement, because there is one more admission to make: if I am honest with myself I have never been truly objective about Stripe specifically, for three reasons.

First, Stripe is a foundational business for my business. The then-startup launched the Subscription API (what later became Stripe Billing ) in late 2011; Stratechery was predicated on that feature existing (and, I would add, the fact that a novice developer like myself could incorporate the Subscription API spoke to Stripe’s ease-of-use!).

Second, Stripe is the foundation of Passport, the access management software that undergirds Stratechery, SemiAnalysis’ institutional offerings , and The Ankler ; we have and continue to work with Stripe closely for both Stratechery and Passport.

Third, I have had the good fortune of becoming friends with Patrick and John Collison, who were some of the earliest Stratechery readers and subscribers.

I did always try and set these considerations aside when writing about Stripe; in truth I actually just wrote about Stripe and the fintech space less, as I was cognizant about these informal conflicts.

By the same token, this is exactly why I couldn’t be more thrilled to have Stripe as an exclusive sponsor: if I am informally conflicted, why not make it formal? I actually think this gives me more freedom to write about fintech, not less, because the conflict will be on my sleeve; more than that, however, every ad I run or read is going to be heartfelt: I believe in Stripe, love their service, and while I am being paid for those ads, I will have the satisfaction of truly believing in them as well.

FAQ

That leaves the impact on you, the reader, and I’ve made an FAQ:

Where are ads going to run?

There are three primary places you will see Stripe ads:

There is a “Presented by Stripe” placement on Stratechery, the cover art of the Stratechery, Stratechery Interview, and Sharp Tech podcasts, and in the emails I send. I honestly think it looks pretty great, but I’m biased!

There will be occasional ad placements between sections of the Update, in the Interviews, and between Articles; this will apply to the web, email, and the Stratechery podcast (which is, and will continue to be, simply the audio version of what you can get on the web or via email).

There will be a segment of Sharp Tech where Andrew and I discuss the Stripe ad topic of the week, along with an acknowledgment at the beginning of an episode, and an ad at the end.

More on Sharp Tech below.

What about sponsored content?

There is no requirement that I run sponsored content; however, I’m actually very excited about the potential of occasionally leveraging Stripe content. Stripe has a unique position in terms of working with companies across the entire economy, and that is particularly true when it comes to AI. You see some of the insights that come from this position on both the Stripe blog and the Stripe Economics blog , and I look forward to incorporating those kinds of insights when it makes sense (and I should also call out Stripe’s Works in Progress site ). Just to be clear, however, that will be my call.

So Stripe can’t tell you what to write?

Absolutely not. More than that, Stripe cannot tell me what not to write either. I could call for Patrick Collison’s firing and I’m still going to get paid.

I am not, for the record, going to do that; as I noted I will disclose this relationship whenever it seems relevant. However, my first loyalty is to my readers; that meant absolute editorial independence was a prerequisite for this deal.

Can I skip the ads if I’m a subscriber?

No. Like I said above, Stratechery is a business, and it’s the quality of my audience that makes this deal possible. Moreover, Stratechery has never promised to be ad-free: what I am selling is access to my paid content, and it’s on me to make that content worthwhile. In fact, I would spin this the other way: my motivation to deliver great content is higher than ever, knowing that it has to be worth not just your money but also the attention that I have chosen to share with a sponsor.

That noted, while I don’t make categorical statements about my business, I do not anticipate raising subscription prices again, and certainly not over the course of this deal.

Do I get anything out of this deal?

This is the part I’m most excited about: I am going to invest the revenue from this deal into making more and better products. I have a bunch of ideas that are now unlocked, and one of them is launching this week: in-person Sharp Tech.

The New Sharp Tech

I am extremely excited to announce that, starting this week, Sharp Tech will become a video podcast, recorded live and in-person. Over the past couple of months I have been building a small video studio in my home, and Andrew will be flying to Wisconsin every week (when possible) to make what I strongly believe will be a better product. There is no matching the energy and chemistry that comes from recording in person, so we’re going to do exactly that the majority of the time.

We will be posting video episodes on YouTube (for clarity, not live as we record, at least to start), as well as through existing feeds; these episodes will be free. In addition, we will be adding a second weekly mailbag-centric audio-only episode — recorded the same day, in-person — for subscribers only.

This is the first of what I hope will be many product launches for subscribers; my goal is that this sponsorship is seen as a real unlock and accelerant for what it means to be not just a subscriber but a member of the best audience in the world. That’s what I believe I have, it’s what Stripe believes that I have, and I’m grateful to every one of you for making that a reality and this business possible.
